desc:
You are given a strictly increasing integer array nums and a positive integer diff. Count the index triples i < j < k such that nums[j] - nums[i] = diff and nums[k] - nums[j] = diff.

For example, nums = [0, 1, 4, 6, 7, 10] and diff = 3 give 2, from the triples of values (1, 4, 7) and (4, 7, 10).
constraints: 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10<sup>9</sup>, and nums is strictly increasing
hints: Three nested loops are far too slow for 10,000 elements. Fix the smallest element of the triple; do the other two values follow?
Since the array is strictly increasing, all values are distinct, so a value x determines a unique triple (x, x + diff, x + 2 * diff).
Put all values in a set. For every x in the array, add 1 to the answer when both x + diff and x + 2 * diff are in the set.
editorial: Because the values are distinct, each value occurs at exactly one index, and because the array is increasing, the indices of x, x + diff and x + 2 * diff are automatically in order. So the number of triples equals the number of values x whose two successors in the progression also appear in the array.

Build a hash set once, then test two memberships per element: O(n) time and O(n) space. A three-pointer sweep over the sorted array reaches O(1) extra space, but the set is simpler and just as fast in practice.
